references.text: Describes how the fat is removed from the peace offering (זֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים), which follows the same procedure referred to in Leviticus 4:31.
Parallel text stating that the priest shall burn the fat on the altar and make atonement, with a promise of forgiveness.
Nearly identical wording regarding the removal of fat, burning it on the altar, making atonement, and receiving forgiveness for the sin offering.
The expression 'a pleasing aroma to the Lord' (לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ לַיהוָה) is also used here concerning the burnt offering.
Refers to the priest's sprinkling of blood and burning of fat as a pleasing aroma to the Lord.
Early use of the expression 'a pleasing aroma to the Lord' in connection with the burnt offering.
The priest makes atonement for one who has sinned unintentionally, and that person receives forgiveness (וְנִסְלַח).
Explains that under the law nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness—fulfilling the principle of atonement from Leviticus.
Contrasts the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant with Christ's final sacrifice, showing that animal blood could not completely take away sins.
